lede: Push something heavy and it shifts slowly; push something light with the same effort and it shoots away. Newton's second law puts a number on that. Unit 2 uses it on boxes dragged along a level floor, often by a rope at an angle, and inside its connected-body and slope questions.
can: Find the resultant force along the line of motion and use it in $F = ma$
Put the mass in the equation and the weight on the diagram
Split a pull at an angle into the part that drives and the part that lifts

md: $F = ma$ is on the Unit 2 sheet, and its $F$ is the **resultant**: what is left along the line of motion once every force there is counted with its sign, a force against the motion counting minus. The dashed arrow on the diagram marks the acceleration. It is not a force, so it never goes into the resultant.

stem: The box in the diagram has mass 16 kg. It is pulled by 100 N against a resistance of 20 N. Calculate its acceleration.

steps.decision: Along the line of motion, with the direction of motion positive: the resistance acts backwards, so it is taken off.
$F = ma$, with the resultant as $F$ and the mass as $m$.
Divide by the mass. Positive, so the box speeds up the way it is moving.

prompt: A trolley is pushed by 55 N against a resistance of 15 N. What resultant force goes into $F = ma$, in newtons?
explain: Take the resistance off the push, as step 1 of See it did with $100 - 20$: $55 - 15 = 40$ N. Adding them would treat the resistance as helping, and 55 N alone ignores it.

twin.prompt: A cart is pulled by 38 N against a resistance of 11 N. What resultant force goes into $F = ma$, in newtons?
twin.explain: $38 - 11 = 27$ N: the resistance acts against the pull, so it comes off.

text: The mass goes in, not the weight

md: The 16 kg box weighs $16 \times 10 = 160$ N: that is the downward arrow on the diagram. The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass, in kilograms. Put the weight in its place and every acceleration comes out ten times too small, the slip the 2019 report found on this step.

title: Why the two cannot be swapped
md: Mass is how much matter there is; weight is how hard gravity pulls on it. $F = ma$ asks how hard a body is to accelerate, which depends on the matter, so the mass belongs in it.

stem: The same box: a resultant of 80 N, a mass of 16 kg and a weight of 160 N. Which number does the 80 N go with?

steps.decision: The weight is gravity's pull, in newtons: it belongs on the diagram.
The equation of motion takes the mass: how much matter has to be sped up.
Dividing by the weight is the ten-times-too-small slip.

prompt: A block of mass 3.5 kg, weight 35 N, feels a resultant force of 21 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: The $m$ in $F = ma$ is the mass, 3.5 kg, as step 2 of See it used 16 and not 160: $21 = 3.5a$, so $a = 6$ m/s². Dividing by the weight, 35, gives 0.6, ten times too small.

twin.prompt: A sack of mass 9 kg, weight 90 N, feels a resultant force of 27 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
twin.explain: $27 = 9a$, so $a = 3$ m/s²: the mass goes in, not the 90 N weight.

text: Name the body, then four lines

md: The 2019 report saw one body's forces mixed up with a whole system's. Start every equation by naming the body and its positive direction. Then write the resultant, then $= ma$, then the answer: four lines, and the equation line keeps its mark even if the division then slips.

stem: A 22 kg crate is dragged by 95 N against a resistance of 29 N. Calculate its acceleration.

steps.working: For the crate, with its direction of motion positive:
steps.decision: Name the body first, so only its own forces go in.
Take the resistance off the pull.
The equation line: write it even when the numbers look awkward.
Divide by the mass.

title: Newton's 2nd Law of Motion, F = ma
why: The same law at a slower pace, with the resultant formed before anything else. It is an A level video, so stop before any coefficient of friction appears: CCEA never uses one.

prompt: A chest of mass 8 kg is dragged by 65 N against a resistance of 25 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
explain: The same four lines as See it: for the chest, $65 - 25 = 40$ N, then $40 = 8a$, so $a = 5$ m/s².

twin.prompt: A trunk of mass 25 kg is dragged by 160 N against a resistance of 60 N. What is its acceleration, in m/s²?
twin.explain: For the trunk: $160 - 60 = 100$ N, then $100 = 25a$, so $a = 4$ m/s².

md: CCEA never tests $F = \mu R$. Friction arrives as a plain value or as **so many newtons per kilogram**, and the second form is a one-step conversion: multiply by the mass. It looks like a coefficient and it is not one. Give the conversion its own line: it carries its own mark.

stem: A 14 kg trolley is pushed by 70 N against a resistance of 2 N per kg. Calculate its acceleration.

steps.decision: Every kilogram is resisted by 2 N, so multiply by the mass.
The resultant along the floor equals mass times acceleration.
42 divided by 14.

prompt: A resistance of 5 N per kg acts on a sledge of mass 9 kg. What is the resisting force, in newtons?
explain: Multiply by the mass, as step 1 of See it did: $5 \times 9 = 45$ N. The 5 N is the pull on one kilogram only.

twin.prompt: A resistance of 6 N per kg acts on a cart of mass 7 kg. What is the resisting force, in newtons?
twin.explain: $6 \times 7 = 42$ N: every one of its 7 kilograms is resisted by 6 N.

md: Vertical motion is the same equation with the weight in it. Choose a direction, say so, and write the resultant in that direction: with up positive, the tension minus the weight. A positive answer means the acceleration is upwards; a negative one means downwards.

stem: A lift of mass 700 kg hangs on a cable with tension 7560 N. Find its acceleration.

steps.decision: The weight in newtons, for the diagram and the resultant.
The tension pulls up and counts plus; the weight pulls down and counts minus.
Positive with up positive, so the acceleration is upwards: say so.

prompt: A lift of mass 300 kg hangs on a cable with tension 3300 N. Taking up as positive, which equation is right?
explain: With up positive the tension counts plus and the weight minus, as in step 2 of See it. The weight is $300 \times 10 = 3000$ N, so the equation is $3300 - 3000 = 300a$.

twin.prompt: A lift of mass 450 kg hangs on a cable with tension 4200 N. Taking up as positive, which equation is right?
twin.explain: Tension up, weight down: the weight is $450 \times 10 = 4500$ N, larger than the tension, so $a$ comes out negative and the acceleration is downwards.

optionNotes.why: It leaves the weight out, but gravity pulls down on the lift the whole time, so the resultant is the tension minus the weight.
It takes off the mass, 450, where the weight in newtons belongs: 450 times 10 is 4500.
It leaves the weight out, but gravity pulls down on the lift the whole time, so the resultant is the tension minus the weight.
It takes off the mass, 300, where the weight in newtons belongs: 300 times 10 is 3000.

md: A rope at an angle $\theta$ above the floor does two jobs. Its part along the floor, $P\cos\theta$, drives the box; its part upwards, $P\sin\theta$, lifts a little of the box's weight. Only the first goes into $F = ma$, because the box moves along the floor.

stem: A rope pulls a box with 30 N at 20° above the horizontal. Find the parts of the pull along the floor and straight up.

steps.decision: The side next to the angle takes the cosine.
The side opposite the angle takes the sine.

prompt: A rope pulls a sledge with 20 N at 30° above the horizontal. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
explain: The part along the ground is next to the angle, so it takes the cosine, as step 1 of See it did: $20\cos 30° = 17.32$ N. The sine gives 10 N, the part that lifts.

twin.prompt: A rope pulls a sled with 35 N at 15° above the horizontal. What is the part of the pull along the ground, in newtons, to 2 decimal places?
twin.explain: Next to the angle, so the cosine: $35\cos 15° = 33.81$ N.

md: The rope carries part of the weight, so the floor pushes back with less than the whole weight. Vertically nothing accelerates: the reaction and the rope's upward part together hold up the weight. Writing $R$ as the weight, or as the rope's upward part alone, lost the reaction marks in 2019 and 2023.

stem: A 6 kg box on a rough level floor is pulled by 30 N at 20° above the horizontal against friction of 8 N. Find the normal reaction and the acceleration.

steps.decision: Nothing moves up or down, so the upward forces balance the weight.
Only the rope's part along the floor drives; the friction opposes it.
Divide by the mass, not the weight.

prompt: An 8 kg block on a level floor is pulled along by a string at 30° above the horizontal with a tension of 90 N. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
explain: Nothing accelerates vertically, so $R$ and the string's upward part hold up the weight, as in step 1 of See it: $90\sin 30° = 45$ N, so $R + 45 = 80$ and $R = 35$ N.

twin.prompt: A 9 kg crate on a level floor is pulled along by a rope at 30° above the horizontal with a tension of 16 N. What is the normal reaction, in newtons?
twin.explain: The rope's upward part is $16\sin 30° = 8$ N, so $R = 90 - 8 = 82$ N.

md: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so there is no $ma$: the resultant is zero and the forces along the floor balance. With a pull at an angle, its part along the floor equals the friction. Summer 2023 Q3 asked exactly this, and many looked for an acceleration that was not there.

stem: A 9 kg block is dragged at a constant velocity by a rope pulling 40 N at 20° above the horizontal. Find the friction on it.

steps.decision: No change of speed means no resultant along the floor.
The pull's part along the floor balances the friction.
The friction equals the pull's part along the floor.

prompt: A block is dragged along a rough floor by a rope and moves at a constant velocity. What is the resultant force on the block?
options: Zero, so the forces along the floor balance
The rope's pull along the floor
answer: Zero, so the forces along the floor balance
explain: Constant velocity means $a = 0$, as step 1 of See it said, so the resultant is $m \times 0 = 0$ and the forces along the floor balance. The pull along the floor is cancelled by the friction, and mass times speed is not a force at all.

twin.prompt: A sledge is pulled across snow at a constant velocity by a horizontal rope. How does the pull compare with the friction?
options: They are equal, so the resultant is zero
The pull is larger, or the sledge would not move
The friction is larger, because the snow slows it
twin.answer: They are equal, so the resultant is zero
twin.explain: Constant velocity means no acceleration, so no resultant: the pull and the friction balance exactly. A larger pull would make the sledge speed up.

optionNotes.option: The pull is larger, or the sledge would not move
optionNotes.why: A larger pull would make the sledge speed up; to keep moving at a steady speed it needs no resultant at all.

optionNotes.option: The friction is larger, because the snow slows it
optionNotes.why: A larger friction would slow the sledge down, but its velocity is constant, so the two forces balance.
Mass times speed is not a force; the resultant is mass times acceleration, and the acceleration here is zero.

optionNotes.option: The rope's pull along the floor
optionNotes.why: The pull along the floor is cancelled by the friction, so together they leave no resultant at all.

md: **Show that** (2022, 2024, 2026). A value is printed for you to reach. Form the equation with the letter still in it and solve forwards; putting the printed value in and checking earned nothing in 2022 and at most two marks in 2024.

**Something changes** (2022, 2023). A later part swaps the load, the pull or the friction: write the equation again with the new mass or force in every place it appears. **How fast, or how far** (2019): the acceleration goes into a constant-acceleration formula, with $u = 0$ from rest.

stem: A lift of mass $M$ kg is pulled up by a cable with tension 5460 N and accelerates upwards at 0.5 m/s². Show that $M = 520$.

steps.decision: The resultant upwards equals mass times acceleration, with M still a letter.
Collect the M terms on one side.
The printed value arrives last, as the result of the working.

prompt: A part says 'Show that the mass of the lift is 520 kg'. Which route earns full marks?
options: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
Putting 520 into the equation and showing both sides agree
Writing down 520 kg with its units
answer: Forming the equation of motion and solving it for the mass
explain: A show-that is marked on the derivation: the equation built from the forces with $M$ still in it, the $M$ terms collected, then solved, as See it reached 520 on its last line. Putting the value in and checking is verification, capped at two marks.

twin.prompt: A part says 'Show that the tension is 3900 N'. Which route earns full marks?
options: Forming the equation of motion with $T$ in it and solving it
Putting 3900 into the equation and showing both sides agree
twin.answer: Forming the equation of motion with $T$ in it and solving it
twin.explain: The marks are for the derivation: the equation with the letter in it, then its solution. Checking the printed value is verification, capped at two marks.

optionNotes.option: Putting 3900 into the equation and showing both sides agree
optionNotes.why: That checks the answer rather than finding it, which CCEA caps at two marks.
The printed value earns nothing on its own: the marks are for the equation and its solution.

optionNotes.option: Putting 520 into the equation and showing both sides agree
optionNotes.why: That checks the answer rather than finding it, which CCEA caps at two marks.

optionNotes.option: Writing down 520 kg with its units
optionNotes.why: The printed value earns nothing on its own: the marks are for the equation and its solution.

md:
Form the resultant along the line of motion before using $F = ma$.
Put the mass in the equation and the weight on the diagram.
Turn a resistance per kilogram into one force, and write a lift's equation with its direction.
Split a pull at an angle: $P\cos\theta$ drives, $P\sin\theta$ lightens the reaction.
Spot the twists: a steady speed, a show-that, a change of load, a formula after.

When this has a question of its own (Q3 in 2019, 2022 and 2023) it is a block on a level floor, often pulled at an angle: the forces, the normal reaction, the acceleration, then a change or a formula after. The equation earns one mark for the resultant along the floor and one for $= ma$. Stuck? Write *for the block:*, then resolve the pull.
